The tradition calls God *the living God*, not merely existent but supremely alive, life in its highest instance. The difficulty is what *life* has meant since the tradition's own founding texts: to be alive is to move from within, to act of oneself, to be the source of one's own activity rather than a thing merely held in being. The classical God, though, is pure act without potency, immutable, outside time: a being that passes from no state of activity to any other. The predicate that was to mark God as most alive turns out to require the very self-movement the surrounding attributes deny.

*What the tradition holds.* Scripture's God is *the living God*, and the philosophical tradition makes life a divine attribute of the first rank. Aristotle's unmoved mover is itself life: the actuality of thought is life, and God is that actuality. The divine life is the eternal self-contemplation of *noēsis noēseōs*, thought thinking itself (Aristotle, *Metaphysics* [-@aristotle1984, XII.7, XII.9]). Aquinas systematizes the attribution: life belongs to God most properly of all, because those things are most properly called living that move themselves. Life is immanent self-activity, operation that proceeds from the agent and remains within it, and God, as pure act, is the highest instance of such immanent operation, the act of self-understanding (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.18.1–4]). To live is the highest grade of being; God, as the fullness of being, is alive in the fullest sense: *vita Dei*, the life identical with the divine essence. The doctrine keeps the God of the covenant from collapsing into an inert principle by binding life to actuality: God is most alive because most fully in act.

*What cannot be answered.* Four questions ask of the doctrine what it cannot answer once *life* is required to carry its own content. The pressure beneath them is that the tradition's own definition of life (immanent self-movement) names the transition the classical attributes forbid.

**Q1.** *If to be alive is to move oneself, and God cannot change, what makes God living rather than inert?* Aquinas defines the living as the self-moving (*ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.18.1]): self-movement is a passage from one state of activity to another effected by the thing itself. The classical God is immutable and timeless: it undergoes no transition, effects no change in itself, passes from no state to any other. A being in which nothing moves satisfies the definition of the inert, not the living; the tradition's own criterion for life is the one the classical God is built to fail. The reply that divine "movement" is metaphorical (activity without change) either keeps the content of *self-movement*, and immutability is lost, or drops it, and *living* no longer marks anything off from a static principle.

**Q2.** *If God's life is the pure actuality of self-understanding, what does that understanding do that bare being does not already do?* Aristotle and Aquinas locate the divine life in contemplation: the changeless act of thought thinking itself. The Thomist anticipates the obvious pressure (that an act which never passes from considering to considered is an act in name only) and blocks it on the doctrine's own terms: *life* and *operation* are predicated of God not univocally but analogically (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.13]), naming *immanent operation*, activity that remains wholly within the agent and needs no transition, in a mode proper to the divine being. It is the strongest reply the doctrine has here, and it has to be met where §5.2.1 meets it. Analogical predication earns its content only if the predicate tracks a real correlate in the divine subject, standing in the appropriate proportion to its creaturely instance (§5.2.1); a predicate that tracks no such correlate is not analogical but empty. Ask what the correlate of *operation* is. The Thomist denies at the outset that divine understanding is a taking-up that runs from understanding to understood: in God knower and known coincide, the operation remaining wholly within, with no interval to cross and no order to run. Grant exactly that. The pressure is not that God's self-understanding *must* be a directed crossing, but that it must be *something* if it is to be operation at all: an exercise the divine subject performs, tellable apart from the bare standing of its essence. And §5.3.3 fixes what any such exercise costs: an interval across which it runs (S), an order in the running (T), and a substantial carrier in which it originates and terminates (Φ). The dilemma is therefore not whether the divine act crosses an interval the Thomist has already denied, but whether, stripped of every such condition, anything is left that *operation* still names. The horns are the ones §5.2.1 draws for *actus purus*: either the divine operation is a genuine way of being-in-act, and it carries the conditions any way of being decomposes into, or it is no way at all (an act with no exercise, no relatum, no passage) and then it is indistinguishable from the bare standing of the essence, and *life* has added nothing to *existence*.

**Q3.** *If God is alive only by being responsive to what happens, how can the living God be the ground of happening rather than a participant in it?* The process tradition presses exactly this: the immutable, impassible God is *dead* (affected by nothing, responsive to nothing) and only a God who genuinely changes with the world is alive [@hartshorne1948]. The dipolar God is alive because responsive. But §5.3.3 has shown what responsiveness costs: to receive and respond is to stand in a directed crossing that runs through T, S, and Φ, and a being alive by such crossing instantiates the structural conditions rather than standing beyond them. Life bought by responsiveness is life on the structure's terms. The horns are fixed: an unresponsive God keeps aseity and forfeits life; a responsive God secures life and forfeits aseity.

**Q4.** *If God's life, knowledge, will, and being are one undivided act, what does calling God living add to calling God existent?* On divine simplicity (§5.2.1), God's life is not distinct from God's understanding, willing, or being: God *is* the divine life, without composition. But then *living* marks no feature that could be present or absent, and §5.2.1 has traced where that leads. Either *life* picks out a determinate content distinct from bare existence, an operation tellable apart from the mere standing of the essence, and the simplicity that forbids all internal differentiation fails; or it picks out nothing distinguishable, and *the living God* says no more than *the existing God*, the predicate emptied of the vitality it was asserted to carry.

*What is required.* The four pressures together isolate what *life* depends on. Life, on the tradition's own definition, is immanent self-movement, and self-movement requires a before-and-after of the moving (T), differentiated states between which the living thing passes (S), and a substantial agent that persists as the source of its own activity across the passage (Φ). Contemplation counts as life only where it is exercised, and an exercise stripped of interval, order, and carrier has yet to show what *operation* still names. Responsiveness counts as life only at the cost of embedding in the structure the response crosses. And life predicates something of its bearer only where it is distinguishable from bare existence, which requires the composition simplicity denies. What *life* survives as, once the pressures have run, is not a grade of being a static essence could hold but the structural fact of a carrier in directed activity among its states.

*What is inverted.* Life is the self-activity of Substance in time. *Living*, in the only sense that survives, names a carrier (Φ) undergoing directed transition (T) among differentiated states (S) from an internal principle, which is to say, it names Nature in act. Aristotle sees it exactly: the actuality of thought is life, and actuality, as the argument has shown, is the instantiation of the structural conditions, not their negation. The tradition reaches for *life* to say that God is no inert abstraction but the living source of all activity; traced honestly, the same vocabulary finds that what is alive is what moves itself through time, and what moves itself through time is Nature, not a being defined by the denial of motion. The living God is the life of Nature, named as though it stood outside the only thing that lives. The predicate is inverted from within: *the living God* is a being specified by the absence of everything living things do.
